traits: Yellowing patches that start in the sunniest, driest spots and spread outward
Damage looks like drought stress but doesn't green up after watering
Adults about 3-4 mm (under 1/5 inch), black body, white wings with a small dark spot on the margin
Part the grass at the patch edge — tiny black bugs with white wing marks

look_alikes.difference: Chinch bugs are black with a small dark wing-margin spot and kill turf; big-eyed bugs have noticeably large eyes and are a beneficial predator, not a pest.
look_alikes.next_photo: The closest possible photo of the insect on a blade of grass, next to a coin.

copy.what_it_means: The #1 killer of St. Augustine lawns in Florida. The tell: drought stress recovers with water, chinch damage doesn't. They kill outward from the first patch, so the earlier it's caught the better the lawn's chances; extensive dead patches may need resodding rather than just treatment.
copy.fact: The #1 killer of St. Augustine lawns in Florida. The tell: drought stress recovers with water, chinch damage doesn't.
copy.blurb: Southern chinch bugs kill St. Augustine grass in expanding yellow-to-brown patches, usually starting in the sunniest, driest spots.

tech_notes: Float test at patch margin (not center) — insert a topless can, fill with water 5 min, bugs float up. Distinguish drought stress first; treat margins outward per label.

traits: White foam blobs on grass stems — the nymphs' bubble shelters
Adults 6-12 mm, dark brown to black with two reddish-orange lines across the wings
Grass develops purple, red, or white streaking, then yellows and browns
Nymphs inside the foam are pale yellow-green, wingless, and much smaller than the adults

look_alikes.difference: Spittlebugs leave white foam and leaf streaking; chinch bugs cause drought-like patches with tiny black bugs at the soil line, no foam.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the grass blades showing foam (or streaking) versus bare patches.

copy.what_it_means: The "spit" is a bubble tent the nymph builds around itself for moisture and protection while it feeds. Light foam here and there is cosmetic; widespread streaking plus browning across the lawn is worth treating.
copy.fact: The "spit" is a bubble tent the nymph builds around itself for moisture and protection.
copy.blurb: Light foam is cosmetic; widespread stripes-and-foam plus browning is treatable.

tech_notes: Confirm foam nymphs + adult two-line pattern. Second generation (Jul-Aug) causes most turf damage; treat per label if streaking spreads.

traits: Shield-shaped body, roughly 12-13 mm, green or brown depending on species
Found year-round on vegetable and ornamental plants, especially tomatoes and beans
Releases a defensive odor from thorax glands when crushed or handled
Occasionally wanders indoors around doors and windows

look_alikes.difference: Stink bugs have a plain shield outline; leaf-footed bugs have a flattened, leaf-like flare on the hind legs.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up from above of the hind legs and overall body outline, next to a coin.

copy.what_it_means: In Southwest Florida, stink bugs are year-round garden feeders on tomatoes and other plants, not the cold-weather wall-sitters seen up north. They occasionally wander indoors around doors and windows; sealing gaps helps, and heavy vegetable damage is worth a look.
copy.fact: The smell is a defense chemical from glands on the thorax — vacuuming rather than squishing avoids it.
copy.blurb: Southwest Florida's stink bugs are year-round garden feeders on tomatoes and other vegetables, not the cold-weather wall-sitters found up north. Sealing door and window gaps helps keep wandering ones outside.

tech_notes: SWFL pentatomids (southern green stink bug, brown stink bug) are year-round plant/fruit feeders — distinguish from the northern brown marmorated stink bug's cold-weather wall-aggregation behavior, which isn't established here. Exclusion (weatherstripping, screens) for occasional indoor wanderers; garden-side treatment per label if vegetable damage is heavy.
